title: Do Big Lever Governments or States help learning happen or do they get in the way?
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton introduces a distinction between big levers, system-wide decisions, and little levers, the moment-by-moment choices of people on the ground, using hotels, petrol stations and traffic lights as illustrations. He notes that trouble often arises because lever-pullers at each level do not understand each other, as in tension between central finance teams and school staff. He lists six examples of government-level education levers and then examines English school inspection against two questions: was it implemented, and did it bring benefits. He finds every benefit paired with a downside, such as stress and complacency, and defers the key question of effects on learning to the following week.
points: Big levers set the system and little levers decide how it plays out, and problems arise when the two do not understand each other's position.
Governments cannot pull little levers because they lack classroom context, while teachers lack the system-wide view.
English school inspections have probably cut the number of really bad schools, but have also wasted emotional energy and sometimes had tragic outcomes.
Big-lever policies typically bring unintended downsides at least as large as their benefits.
The question that matters, whether such policies help or hinder learning, is left to a follow-up post.
quotes: The big levers that are pulled are the decisions that are made with the intention of changing the focus or operation of the whole system. The little levers that are pulled are the decisions that are made everywhere in the organisation that affect moment by moment practice.

Quite often, some of the problems that exist in organisations are that those pulling the big levers and those pulling the little levers have little awareness of each other’s position or contribution to the whole organisation. That’s when we hear the complaints from staff on the ground that ‘It would be a lot better if those people in central office actually knew what was going on here in the factory’.

Governments can’t pull the little levers because they don’t know the context of individual situations, in the classroom. They rely on accumulating large amounts of evidence that tell them what the patterns are system-wide.
The inspection system has almost certainly reduced the number of really bad schools that exist in England. This may be the single biggest benefit of the whole system.

But it has also caused other schools and school faculties to waste huge amounts of emotional energy wondering if they will comply well enough with the system. Very occasionally, these worries have had tragic outcomes.

But some schools have then become complacent and sat on their laurels, only to find four years later when the next inspection comes round that they are no longer ‘outstanding’ even within the context of the inspection system, with inevitable internal and public confusion, disappointment and concern.

Like all big lever issues, though, these benefits come with either unintended negative outcomes that no one realised beforehand or they come with downsides which are at least equal to if not worse than the benefits.
